title: Genesis 33. The Cup of Reconciliation.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 33. The Cup of Reconciliation.
Jacob lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, Esau was coming.
And with him four hundred men.
The brother is here.
The last time they stood face to face,
Jacob was running for his life.
Esau had said in his heart:
Let the days of mourning for my father approach.
Then I will kill my brother Jacob.
That was twenty years ago.
The threat has had twenty years to cool, or to harden.
And now Esau is coming with four hundred men.
Jacob divided the children.
The servants and their children first.
Leah and her children next.
Rachel and Joseph last.
The order reveals the heart.
The beloved wife and her son are kept furthest from danger.
The same favoritism that defined his parents' household, Isaac loving Esau,
Rebekah loving Jacob, now defines Jacob's.
The man who suffered under divided love now divides his own family by the same measure.
The Cup is held by a vessel that repeats the crack it inherited.
He himself passed over before them and bowed himself to the ground seven times,
until he came near to his brother.
Seven bows.
The man who stole the blessing now prostrates himself seven times before the brother he wronged.
The grabber bows.
The one who took by deception now approaches by submission.
Each bow closes the distance.
Each prostration says: I am not your lord.
I am your servant.
The stolen blessing, be lord over your brothers,
let your mother's sons bow to you, is now reversed.
The brother who was told he would be lord is now on his face in the dirt.
And Esau ran to meet him.
Not Jacob, Esau.
The wronged brother runs.
The one who was robbed, who wept, who planned murder,
who came with four hundred men, runs.
The four hundred do not advance in formation.
Esau does not wait for Jacob to finish bowing.
He runs.
He embraced him.
He fell on his neck.
He kissed him.
They wept.
The first fully visible reconciliation in Genesis.
Not a covenant between men who do not trust each other,
like Abraham and Abimelech.
Not a boundary of stones, like Jacob and Laban.
An embrace.
A kiss.
Tears.
The wronged brother initiates.
The energy of forgiveness comes from the one who was wronged.
Esau lifted up his eyes and saw the women and children.
He said: Who are these with you?
Jacob said: The children whom God has graciously given your servant.
Your servant.
The one who took the master's blessing now calls himself servant to the one he took it from.
The concubines and their children bowed.
Leah and her children bowed.
Then Joseph came near with Rachel, and they bowed.
The family that was hidden behind tents and arranged in order of preference is now fully visible.
No more disguise.
No more goatskin.
No more servants between them.
The man who deceived his father's face now shows his own.
Esau said:
What do you mean by all this company which I met?
Jacob said: To find favor in the sight of my lord.
Esau said: I have enough, my brother.
Let what you have be yours.
I have enough.
The brother who was robbed says: I have enough.
The firstborn who lost the birthright says: keep what you have.
The four hundred men who could destroy are not an army of vengeance.
They are the household of a man who has enough.
The Cup of rivalry that began in the womb,
the children struggled together within her, is drained.
Both are full.
Neither needs to take from the other anymore.
Jacob said: Please, no.
If I have now found favor in your sight,
then receive my present at my hand.
Because I have seen your face,
as one sees the face of God,
and you were pleased with me.
Seeing your face is like seeing God's face.
Jacob has just named the place Peniel because he says:
I have seen God face to face,
and yet my life has been delivered.
Now he says seeing Esau's face is like seeing God's face.
The night encounter flows directly into the morning encounter with his brother.
The text places the two faces beside each other without explaining the wrestler's identity beyond Jacob's own recognition.
Please take the gift that I brought to you,
because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.
The word for gift, is the same word for blessing.
The same word Jacob stole from Esau in chapter twenty-seven.
Now Jacob gives blessing to Esau.
Take my blessing.
The stolen blessing returned.
The Cup of stolen recognition poured back.
The grabber gives.
The taker returns.
Not the birthright, that cannot be returned.
But the blessing, the word, the acknowledgment, the submission,
is given back as a gift.
He urged him, and he took it.
Esau takes the gift.
The brother who said I have enough accepts the blessing from the brother who stole it.
The exchange is complete.
What was taken is now given.
What was stolen is now offered.
The Cup that was held by a grabber is now held by a giver.
The vessel that took by deception now restores by generosity.
Esau said: Let us take our journey, and let us go,
and I will go before you.
Jacob said: My lord knows that the children are tender,
and the flocks and herds with me have their young.
If they are overdriven one day, all the flocks will die.
Please let my lord pass over before his servant,
and I will lead on gently,
according to the pace of the children,
until I come to my lord to Seir.
Esau offered to accompany him.
Jacob declined.
He promised to follow to Seir, and did not go.
The reconciled deceiver still navigates carefully.
The Cup of reconciliation does not erase the pattern of strategic withdrawal.
Reconciliation is real.
Trust is partial.
The embrace was genuine.
The promise was not kept.
The man who wrestled with God and limped away still walks with a limp in his relationships.
Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.
Jacob traveled to Succoth, built himself a house,
and made shelters for his livestock.
Therefore, the name of the place is called Succoth.
The first house Jacob builds.
The sojourner who slept on a stone at Bethel now builds a dwelling.
The man who lived in tents for twenty years under Laban now builds his own structure.
But it is not Canaan yet.
Succoth is still east of the Jordan.
Still not the promised land.
Still not home.
The Cup of sojourning pauses, but it has not arrived.
Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem,
which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan-aram.
He encamped before the city.
He bought the parcel of ground where he had spread his tent from the sons of Hamor,
Shechem's father, for a hundred pieces of money.
The second land purchase in Genesis.
Abraham bought Machpelah, a grave.
Jacob buys a field, for living.
The covenant family now owns two pieces of Canaan:
a tomb and a field.
Death and life.
The first acre was for burial.
The second is for dwelling.
The promise that covers all the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates is now held by two small purchases.
The gap between promise and possession continues.
But the Cup is touching the ground.
He erected an altar there and called it: El Elohe Yisrael, God,
the God of Israel.
The first altar Jacob builds.
At Bethel, he set up a stone and poured oil on it.
He did not build an altar.
Now, after the wrestling, after the limp, after the reconciliation,
after the field, he builds.
And he names it with his new name.
El Elohe Yisrael.
God, the God of Israel.
Not the God of Abraham.
Not the God of Isaac.
The God of Israel.
His own name.
The name given to him at Peniel when the man touched his hip and said:
your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel.
Jacob names God by the name God gave him.
The deceiver who became Israel now worships the God of Israel.
The conditional if of Bethel, if God will be with me,
has become a declaration: God is the God of Israel.
The bargain has become a name.
The vow that started with terms has ended with an altar.
The vessel that held the Cup with a conditional hand now holds it with a wounded hip and a new name and a public confession.
The Cup is not clean.
Rachel still carries the teraphim.
Jacob still did not go to Seir.
The favoritism that divided Isaac's household still divides Jacob's.
The vessel is still mixed, promise and idols, reconciliation and evasion,
faith and fear.
But the altar stands.
The name is spoken.
The God who said I will not leave you has been answered by a man who says:
You are my God.
The Cup of reconciliation holds.
Not because the vessel deserved it.
Not because the wrestling earned it.
Because the One who poured it does not stop pouring.
The brother who was wronged ran.
The brother who wronged bowed.
And between the running and the bowing,
between the embrace and the tears,
the Cup that was stolen was returned,
not as a theft but as a gift.
Take my blessing.
And he took it.
